newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND - Gas in Britain faces hectic start to 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Gas in Britain faces hectic start to 1997.

text.p: The New Year for Britain's natural gas industry will be frenzied in the first months, after which the tempo will slow right down -- if the industry comes through the winter unscathed.
In January and February, the whole policy of gas market deregulation will come under scrutiny.
The Network Code, which governs transmission of gas by competing shippers on the British Gas pipeline system, will face its first full winter test.

Domestic competition will increase with a second pilot area, covering 1.5 million householders in Dorset, the former county of Avon, Kent and East and West Sussex, opening for competition in two stages on February 10 and March 7.
London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) will start Europe's first natural gas futures trading contract on January 31.

And British Gas itself will decide at a shareholder's meeting on February 12 if it is to demerge. If that is approved, shares in Centrica, a new company responsible for sales and trading, services and retail businesses as well as the Morecambe Bay gas fields will start trading on February 17.

"The year looks very front-loaded," said analyst Julian Kennedy of consultants Wood Mackenzie. "It puts a lot of emphasis on January and February, and the Network Code will certainly be found out in the first couple of months". NETWORK CODE FACES TEST AFTER GLASGOW BLACKOUT
The first winter of the Network Code will be critical to public confidence.
"There were times last year when it was threatened the lights might go out," said Kennedy. "This year could put it to the test".

TransCo, British Gas' transmission division has said that last winter a cold snap caused it to interrupt supply to all customers in Scotland with interruptible contracts -- which cost less but can be cut off at times of exceptional demand .
But in addition over 4,000 householders near Glasgow were also switched off for five days as pressure dropped.
"Supplies to the whole of Glasgow were very much on the margins," said TransCo's Andy McPhee.

A spokesman for regulator Ofgas would not speculate on the possible consequences if a major supply failure occurs this winter, but was satisfied that Glaswegian customers had been properly looked after. MORE SUPPLY CHOICE FOR MORE HOUSEHOLDERS

The second pilot area to be opened to domestic competition in southern England follows a pilot scheme from April this year when 500,000 householders in Devon, Somerset and Cornwall were given the chance to buy gas from any supplier.
Over 80,000 have so far done so, with at least one new supplier predicting the number will reach 100,000, or 20 percent of the total, by the end of the year.
Eastern Natural Gas, a subsidiary of Hanson Plc, has already signed up over 27,000 customers in the new area.

The whole of Britain, nearly 19 million households, will be open to competition during 1998. But analysts expect a pause before competition extends further. BG DEMERGER AND LONDON FUTURES TRADE ON THE CARDS
The IPE's futures contract, set for launch on January 31, follows months of wrangling over technical details.

But the exchange is optimistic that the spot market is now sufficiently well established to make futures trade successful. The IPE's Richard Ward points out that the natural gas contract on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) is now the third largest energy futures contract in the world and the most successful derivatives contract launched this decade.
The British Gas demerger in February may lead to renewed efforts to renegotiate burdensome contracts, analysts believe.
BG has also reached agreement with both British Petroleum and its own exploration and production arm over 293 million stg of long term take-or-pay contracts.

Chairman Richard Giordano said that this represented some 10 percent of all contracts that the company particularly wanted to renegotiate, and analysts expect a concerted effort to complete more negotiations before the split. MORE SUPPLY IMMINENT IF DISPUTES SETTLED
New gas supply will come next year from British Gas' North Sea Armada field, due onstream in October. Output is expected to reach 450 million cubic feet a day.
Supply could also come from two further sources currently held up by legal wrangles.

Phillips is in dispute with contractual buyer Enron Corp over gas output. Enron has nominated its requirements at zero until 1998, effectively preventing Phillips from proceeding with development of oil from the fields. The two are engaged in litigation in London, and future developments will hinge on the outcome of their case.

Britain and Norway are also back in discussions in a dispute over gas pipelines from the Frigg field, which straddles their territorial waters. The field is connected to Scotland, but under an intergovernmental treaty Norway can only deliver through this pipe from Frigg itself or its satellites.
As Frigg is depleting, Norway is pushing to deliver gas from other fields down the line, which the U.K. has so far resisted.

But if the treaty is renegotiated next year, analysts warn that new gas from this pipeline and from Armada could lead to a bottleneck in the British system. MORE GAS POWER PLANTS OPEN AS EUROPEAN MARKET BECKONS
Further gas-fired power generating capacity is due onstream when National Power opens its 1400 megawatt (MW) Didcot B station in Oxfordshire at the end of the year.

This follows commissioning of Powergen's 1430 MW Connah's Quay earlier this month. Powergen says it has no further construction plans, but gas-fired plant is expected to continue increasing its share of the electricity generating market.
The Dutch presidency of the European Union, for six months from January, is expected to give impetus to development of gas markets in continental Europe.

With the UK-continent gas interconnector pipeline due onstream in 1998, any market deregulation next year may lead shareholders in the interconnector to make fresh efforts to sell gas under contract to European consumers.
"A lot of people in London, like the IPE, are seeing the UK's deregulation as a learning curve", says Kennedy. "The ultimate prize, in Europe, is many times larger."
